questions.question: Describe South Africa's main national roads and transport corridors.
questions.expected_answer: National roads, marked N and managed by SANRAL, some tolled, form the main road network. The N1 runs from Cape Town through the Karoo to Bloemfontein, Johannesburg, Pretoria, Polokwane and Beitbridge on the Zimbabwe border; the N2 follows the south and east coast from Cape Town through Mossel Bay, George, Gqeberha, East London, Mthatha and Durban, then inland to Ermelo; the N3 runs from Durban through Pietermaritzburg and up Van Reenen's Pass to Harrismith and Johannesburg and is the busiest freight route; and the N4 runs from the Botswana border through Rustenburg, Pretoria and Mbombela to Komatipoort and Maputo, partly as the Maputo Development Corridor. Others include the N7 to Namibia, N11, N12 and N14. Corridors are main routes where roads, railways, pipelines and power lines run together, the most important being Durban to Gauteng with the N3, a main railway and the fuel pipeline. The network is densest in Gauteng and thinnest in the Northern Cape and Karoo, and some rural areas still have poor gravel roads.

questions.question: Describe South Africa's railway network and main airports.
questions.expected_answer: The freight railway network of roughly twenty thousand kilometres, the largest in Africa, is run mostly by Transnet Freight Rail and was built from the 1860s to link ports to the diamond fields at Kimberley and the Witwatersrand gold fields, then to coal, iron ore, farming and industry. Main lines radiate from Gauteng to Durban, Cape Town via Kimberley, Gqeberha, East London and Maputo, with heavy-haul lines from Sishen to Saldanha for iron ore and from Mpumalanga to Richards Bay for coal, and links to Botswana, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Namibia, Eswatini and further north. Passenger rail includes PRASA's Metrorail, long-distance trains, the Gautrain and tourist trains. ACSA manages the main airports: O. R. Tambo in Ekurhuleni, the busiest in South Africa, one of Africa's busiest, an international hub and the main air cargo hub; Cape Town International, second busiest, serving tourism and fruit and flower exports; King Shaka near Durban, opened 2010; and others such as Bloemfontein, Gqeberha, East London, George, Kimberley and Upington, with private Lanseria. Airports need large flat sites on city edges with good links, and their noise affects nearby areas.

questions.question: Describe South Africa's commercial harbours and explain the pattern of the transport network.
questions.expected_answer: The eight commercial harbours, managed by Transnet National Ports Authority, are Saldanha Bay, the deepest natural harbour, exporting iron ore; Cape Town, for containers, fruit exports, fishing and ship repair; Mossel Bay, for offshore gas and fishing; Port Elizabeth and the deep-water Port of Ngqura, opened in 2009, for containers, vehicles and manganese; East London, for vehicles and grain; Durban, the busiest, with the most containers, vehicles and fuel; and Richards Bay, a huge coal export terminal also handling minerals and timber. The coastline has few natural harbours, being straight, exposed and with blocked river mouths, so ports needed breakwaters and dredging. The network forms a hub-and-spoke pattern centred on Gauteng because Gauteng grew around the gold mines from 1886 into southern Africa's largest economic area but lies inland about 600 km from Durban, so roads, railways and pipelines link it to the ports, and other mines also needed port links. The network extends to landlocked neighbours and links with Mozambican and Namibian ports, making South Africa a regional transport hub.
